newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Albania situation said improved since troops arrived.
newsitem.headline: Albania situation said improved since troops arrived.

text.p: Albanian U.N. envoy Pellumb Kulla said on Tuesday the situation in his country had improved since the arrival earlier this month of an Italian-led multinational force to protect aid supplies and help promote stability.

"This is a mission of peace, and there has been peace in Albania since the multinational force entered," he told a news conference chaired by Italian ambassador Francesco Paolo Fulci who spearheaed efforts to secure Security Council endorsement of the force.
Kulla said the curfew in Albania was now limited to a few hours, there was no limitation on press freedom and all schools would be open by the end of this month.
"The presence of the multinational force has affected in a good way the everyday life of the population and has also inspired our police and army to be reorganized," he added.

Referring to elections, he said that "all political parties want to go to the ballots on June 29." This meant the election campaign should be proclaimed 45 days in advance, or in about two weeks' time, but there were areas of the country where even the government had no access, he said.

Fulci said the force, which began arriving on April 15 under a three-month U.N. mandate approved on March 28, currently comprised 2,755 Italian troops, 923 from France, 345 from Spain, 630 from Greece, 691 from Turkey and 116 from Austria.
Another 400 soldiers were scheduled to arrive from Romania on May 4 while 60 Danish troops were awaiting authorisation from their parliament.

The force was organised after Albanians took to the streets and raided state arsenals in the chaos that followed the collapse of several get-rich-quick "pyramid" schemes in which many had invested their savings.
Armed rebels, who blame President Sali Berisha for the financial disaster, remain in control of most of the south of the country.
